headline: World Lens Game - Real-Place Image Clues for ESL Speaking
outcomes: Students practise observation language by describing real visual evidence before they guess
Culture, geography, and travel vocabulary become meaningful because students use them to solve a mystery
The reveal creates a natural speaking moment: students compare clues, explain guesses, and notice what they missed
Teachers get a highly visual game that works for online lessons, travel units, and World Flight sessions
howItWorks: Students see image clues from a real place and inspect details such as signs, buildings, weather, landscape, and street life
They make a location guess or discuss likely regions using evidence from the image
LessonCaptain reveals the answer with a pin on the map and a short explanation of the strongest clues
The class scores the round and moves to the next place, building a quick world-tour speaking activity
teacherUseCases: Travel-English warm-up where students practise describing places and giving reasons
A visual speaking game for teens or adults who need more than another grammar prompt
World Flight culture stop: use World Lens before or after arriving in a destination city

faq.q: What language do students practise in World Lens?
faq.a: They practise describing visual evidence, hedging guesses, comparing possibilities, and explaining reasons. Useful phrases include 'It might be...', 'I can see...', 'This suggests...', and 'I changed my mind because...'.

faq.q: Is World Lens suitable for online lessons?
faq.a: Yes. The teacher screen shows the image and reveal while students respond from their own devices or discuss out loud on Zoom, Meet, or Teams.

faq.q: Can one student play World Lens?
faq.a: Yes. One-on-one students can describe what they notice, make a guess, and explain their reasoning. Groups add competition, but the observation task works with a single learner.

faq.q: Does the teacher need to prepare images?
faq.a: No. World Lens is designed around built-in real-place clues. The teacher chooses the lesson context and runs the rounds live.

faq.q: How is World Lens different from a geography quiz?
faq.a: The point is not memorizing capitals. Students solve from evidence, then talk through why the evidence did or did not support their guess. That makes it a speaking and reasoning activity, not just trivia.
